content: Loa loa filariasis is a parasitic disease affecting the skin and eyes, caused by the nematode worm Loa loa. Humans acquire this infection through the bite of certain flies, primarily the horsefly, as well as the deer fly and mango fly. The disease manifests as red, itchy swellings beneath the skin, known as Calabar swellings. The first documented case of Loa loa infection occurred in 1770 in Santo Domingo, in the Caribbean. In 1895, localized angioedema, a hallmark clinical feature of loiasis, was observed in Calabar, a coastal town in Nigeria, giving rise to the term Calabar swellings. However, the connection between Loa loa and these swellings was not established until 1910, when Dr. Patrick Manson identified the association. Loiasis is caused by the nematode Loa loa, which resides in the lymphatic and subcutaneous tissues of humans. Adult worms, approximately 5 mm wide, inhabit the subcutaneous tissues, where they mate and produce microfilariae. These microfilariae are 250–300 μm in length and 6–8 μm in width. They are morphologically distinct from other filariae, as they are sheathed and possess body nuclei that extend to the tip of the tail. The Loa loa parasite is endemic to West and Central Africa. Its geographic distribution spans from southeastern Benin to southern Sudan and Uganda in an east-west direction, and from approximately 10°N latitude to Angola in a north-south direction. It is estimated that between 3 and 13 million people in these regions are infected. Individuals most at risk for loiasis are those living in the high-canopied rainforests of West and Central Africa. The deer flies that transmit the parasite are diurnal biters, with increased activity during the rainy season. These flies are attracted to human movement and smoke from wood fires. Rubber plantations, with their dense tree canopies, create an ideal environment for these flies. Symptoms of loiasis include itchy, non-painful swellings (Calabar swellings) that can occur anywhere on the body, often near joints. Less common symptoms include generalized itching, muscle pain, joint pain, and fatigue. Some infected individuals may remain asymptomatic. Diagnosing loiasis can be challenging, particularly in patients with low levels of microfilariae in the blood. Diagnosis is often initiated when a patient presents with eye worm, Calabar swellings, or unexplained elevated eosinophil levels on blood tests after traveling to an endemic area. Confirmation can be achieved by identifying the adult worm after its removal from under the skin or eye, observing an adult worm in the eye during examination, detecting microfilariae on a blood smear collected between 10 AM and 2 PM, or identifying antibodies against Loa loa. However, serological tests cannot differentiate between active infection and past exposure, and they are not widely available in the United States. Treatment of loiasis involves chemotherapy or, in some cases, surgical removal of adult worms followed by systemic treatment. The drug of choice is diethylcarbamazine (DEC), administered at a dosage of 8–10 mg/kg/day, three times daily for 12 days. The pediatric dosage is the same. DEC is effective against microfilariae and has some efficacy against adult worms. However, in patients with a high microfilarial load, DEC may be contraindicated due to the risk of encephalopathy caused by the rapid killing of microfilariae. In such cases, albendazole is a safer alternative and has shown better outcomes than ivermectin, which, despite its slower microfilaricidal effects, also carries risks. Surgical excision of migrating adult worms is an effective treatment for localized symptoms and provides an opportunity for diagnosis. However, systemic therapy is required to cure the infection unless the patient harbors only a single adult worm. There are no vaccines available to prevent Loa loa infection. Weekly prophylactic administration of DEC (300 mg) is effective in preventing loiasis in long-term travelers to endemic areas. Since deer flies breed in muddy, shaded areas along rivers and are attracted to smoke from wood fires, avoiding these areas can reduce the risk of infection. Personal protective measures, such as using insect repellents like DEET on exposed skin, wearing long sleeves and pants during the day when deer flies are active, and using permethrin-treated clothing, are also recommended.
